quiz.q: Why does Rust lean on the builder pattern instead of what many other languages use for optional constructor arguments?
options: Rust has no constructor overloading or named/optional function arguments
Rust structs cannot have more than 3 fields
Builders are required by the borrow checker
Rust doesn't allow default values anywhere
quiz.explain: Without overloaded constructors or named/optional arguments, a struct with many optional fields needs another way to be built readably — that's what the builder pattern provides.

quiz.q: What must a builder setter method return to support method chaining like `.name("x").port(8080)`?
options: &str
Self
bool
quiz.explain: Each setter takes self (consuming the builder) and must return Self so the next .method() call has something of the right type to call on.

quiz.q: A setter is written as `fn port(mut self, port: u16) { self.port = port; }` (no return type). What happens?
options: It fails to compile at the setter itself with a clear error
It compiles, but the chain breaks at the NEXT method call because port() returns ()
It silently ignores the port value
It automatically infers -> Self
quiz.explain: A function with no declared return type implicitly returns (). The setter itself compiles fine; the error surfaces one call later, when you try to call a method on the () it returned.

quiz.q: Why do required fields in a builder often get stored as `Option<T>` rather than `T`?
options: Option<T> is required by the derive(Default) macro
So .build() can check whether the field was actually set and return an Err if not
Option<T> makes the field mutable
It has no real purpose, it's just convention
quiz.explain: Storing a required field as Option<T> lets .build() distinguish 'never set' (None) from 'set', and use .ok_or(...)? to turn a missing value into a proper Err instead of guessing a default.

quiz.q: What is `.build()` typically responsible for that a plain struct literal isn't?
options: Serializing the struct to JSON
Validating that required fields were provided, often returning a Result
Deleting the builder from memory immediately
Converting all fields to strings
quiz.explain: `.build()` is the natural place to check invariants (required fields present, values in valid ranges) and report failure via Result, since it's the single point where construction actually finishes.

quiz.q: For a struct with only 2-3 non-optional fields, what does the lesson recommend over a full builder?
options: A global mutable variable
Default plus struct-update syntax (..Default::default())
Always still use a builder, no exceptions
Multiple overloaded new() functions
quiz.explain: A builder is overhead for small structs. `Point { x: 10, ..Default::default() }` is simpler and does the same job when there's little real optionality.

quiz.q: Why does a setter take `self` by value instead of `&self`?
options: &self would be a syntax error in impl blocks
Taking self by value lets the method consume and return an updated builder, enabling the chain
Rust requires all methods to take self by value
It has no effect on chaining either way
quiz.explain: Consuming self (mut self) means the method owns the builder for its body and can move a modified version back out via the return value — exactly what chaining `.method().method()` needs.

quiz.q: What's a real-world example of the builder pattern mentioned in the lesson?
options: std::process::Command
std::vec::Vec::new()
println!
std::mem::swap
quiz.explain: std::process::Command is a classic standard-library builder: .arg(), .env(), .current_dir() all chain and return Self, ending in .spawn() or .output().

flashcards.front: Why doesn't Rust use constructor overloading for optional struct fields?
flashcards.back: Rust has no constructor overloading and no named/optional function arguments, so a struct with several optional fields needs another idiomatic way to be constructed readably — the builder pattern.

flashcards.front: What must every setter method in a builder chain return?
flashcards.back: Self. Each setter takes self (or &mut self) and returns Self (or &mut Self) so the next .method() call in the chain has something valid to call on.

flashcards.front: Where does validation of required fields typically happen in the builder pattern?
flashcards.back: In .build(), which checks that required Option<T> fields were set (often with .ok_or(...)?) and returns a Result so missing data becomes a proper Err instead of a silent bug.
For a struct with only 2-3 fields and little real optionality — use Default plus struct-update syntax (..Default::default()) instead.

flashcards.front: What error symptom shows up when a setter forgets to return Self?
flashcards.back: The setter itself compiles fine (it implicitly returns ()), but the NEXT method call in the chain fails with something like 'no method named `X` found for type `()`'.

flashcards.front: Give two real Rust ecosystem examples of the builder pattern.
flashcards.back: reqwest::Client::builder() and std::process::Command — both use chainable setters returning Self, ending in a final consuming call (.build() or .spawn()/.output()).

flashcards.front: What does #[derive(Default)] give a builder struct?
flashcards.back: A default() constructor that sets every field to its type's zero value (0, String::new(), false, None, ...), giving you a clean starting point without writing new() by hand.
